lead: A news sentence says Rao joined TCS in Pune, and a database needs a row: person Rao, employer TCS, city Pune. Information extraction does that reading. It pulls structured records out of free text, and relation extraction is the part that links two named entities into a triple of subject, relation and object. Banks use it to read KYC documents, job portals to parse resumes, and news monitors to build knowledge graphs that answer questions like who works where.
prereq: You need: 2.8 Named entity recognition, because a relation is defined between two entities that have already been found and typed.

blocks.text: Information extraction (IE) takes free text and returns structured records with known fields. A program can then store the record in a table or a graph without reading the sentence again.

The IE family has three members. Entity extraction finds the spans naming people, places, organisations and dates; that is 2.8. Relation extraction takes two entity mentions and decides which relation, if any, holds between them. Template filling, also called slot filling, fills a fixed frame: a job-change record might have the slots PERSON, ORG, LOC and DATE.

The output of relation extraction is a triple (subject, relation, object). Subject and object are entity mentions with their types, and the relation comes from a small closed set such as works_for, based_in or joined_on. (Rao, works_for, TCS) means Rao is employed by TCS.

A set of triples is a knowledge base. Each triple has a head and a tail, so the knowledge base is a directed graph: nodes are entities, labelled edges are relations. Triples sharing an entity join up, so a query like "who works in Pune" becomes a two-hop walk.

Hand-written patterns. Write a regular expression over words or over the POS tags of 2.4. For example, the pattern PER joined ORG in LOC requires all three slots but emits only (PER, works_for, ORG); LOC is kept as context and discarded. This is cheap and needs no training data, but it fires only on the phrasings its author thought of.

Bootstrapping, also called seed-based or semi-supervised learning. Start with a few seed triples. Find sentences where both entities of a seed occur, and take the words between them, or their POS pattern, as a candidate pattern. Keep patterns that match many seeds, apply them to new text to get new pairs, add those pairs to the seed set, and repeat. Precision falls with each round, so stop after a few rounds at a confidence threshold.

Supervised relation classification. Treat each candidate entity pair as one example. Features: the words between the two mentions, their POS tags, the entity types from 2.8, the distance in tokens, which entity comes first, and the head words on the path between them in a parse tree (see Unit 3, Syntax). Train a classifier over labels such as works_for, based_in, lives_in and NONE. NONE matters most, because nearly every entity pair in real text has no relation.
Distant supervision builds training data automatically: align a knowledge base with a corpus and label every sentence containing a known pair with that pair's relation, giving many noisy examples.
Score on held-out text: sentences not used to write the patterns or train the classifier.
P = c / n,   R = c / t,   F1 = 2 × P × R / (P + R)
blocks.where: c is the number of triples produced that match a gold triple exactly; n is the total number of triples produced; t is the number of true relations present in the test text; P is precision, R is recall, F1 is their harmonic mean.

blocks.text: A triple is correct only when subject, relation and object all match the gold triple. Same subject and same relation but a different object is a wrong triple.

Relation extraction assumes the entities are already right. A wrong span, such as a person mention swallowing the verb, or a wrong type, such as TCS tagged as a person, hands the classifier a wrong argument, and the triple is lost even when the relation is recognised. If entity and relation errors are independent, end-to-end F1 is roughly their product: 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.72. Errors stack, they do not cancel.
This closes the subject's sequence: sequence labels (2.4 to 2.7), then entity spans (2.8), then relations between those spans.

figure.caption: One sentence, "Rao joined TCS in Pune last Monday", becomes three triples: (Rao, works_for, TCS), (Rao, works_in, Pune) and (Rao, joined_on, Monday), one arrow each. Every arrow is one row of the knowledge base, and the shared node Rao is what lets a query walk from person to employer to city to date.

spec.aria: A directed graph with node Rao (PER) on the left joined by three labelled arrows: works_for to TCS (ORG), works_in to Pune (LOC) and joined_on to Monday (DATE).

examples.question: The sentence is "Rao joined TCS in Pune last Monday". (a) List the named entities with their types, and the triples the sentence yields. (b) A pattern PER joined ORG in LOC fires on 3 held-out sentences and gives a correct triple on 2 of them. The held-out text contains 5 true relations. Compute precision, recall and F1 for this pattern.
steps: Triples read off the sentence: (Rao, works_for, TCS), (Rao, works_in, Pune), (Rao, joined_on, Monday).
The pattern fired on 3 held-out sentences and produced one triple each, so n = 3 triples produced, of which c = 2 are correct. Precision = c / n = 2 / 3 = 0.67.
examples.answer: Precision 0.67, recall 0.40, F1 0.50 for the pattern on the held-out text.
examples.check:
correct = 2
produced = 3
true_rel = 5
p = correct / produced
r = correct / true_rel
f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r)
print(f"{p:.2f}")
print(f"{r:.2f}")
print(f"{f1:.2f}")

traps: Measuring pattern precision on the sentences you used to write the pattern. Report it on held-out text only.
Counting a triple as correct when the subject and relation match but the object differs. All three parts must match the gold triple.
Confusing relation extraction with entity extraction: relation extraction receives the entities as input, so it cannot repair a wrong span or a wrong entity type.
Reporting recall as the number of patterns or seed pairs. Recall is correct triples divided by all true relations in the text, including those no pattern fires on.
Running bootstrapping for many rounds and quoting the first round's precision. Precision decays as drift enters the seed set.

quiz.q: Define the output triple of relation extraction and name its three parts.
quiz.a: A triple (subject, relation, object): subject and object are typed entity mentions, and relation is a label from a small closed set such as works_for.

quiz.q: Why does relation extraction depend on entity extraction being correct?
quiz.a: A relation is a label on a pair of entity mentions. A wrong boundary or wrong type gives the wrong pair of arguments, so the triple is wrong even if the relation label is right.

quiz.q: Describe the bootstrapping loop for relation extraction and one risk it carries.
quiz.a: Seeds give sentences, sentences give context patterns, patterns give new pairs, new pairs become seeds. Risk: semantic drift, where wrong pairs enter the seed set and precision falls each round.

quiz.q: A pattern produces 8 triples, 6 of which are correct. The held-out text holds 20 true relations. Find precision, recall and F1.
For "Rao joined TCS in Pune last Monday", write the triples and the entity types each one needs.
quiz.a: (Rao, works_for, TCS) needs PER and ORG; (Rao, works_in, Pune) needs PER and LOC; (Rao, joined_on, Monday) needs PER and DATE.

quiz.q: A team reports precision 0.95 and recall 0.20 for hand-written relation patterns. Explain both numbers and give one remedy.
quiz.a: The patterns are narrow: they match only the phrasings written by hand, so nearly every match is right (high precision) but most true relations are missed (low recall). Remedy: bootstrap new patterns from seeds, or train a supervised classifier on labelled pairs.

quiz.q: Entity F1 is 0.90 and relation F1 on gold entities is 0.80. Why is end-to-end relation F1 lower than 0.80?
quiz.a: The relation stage consumes predicted entities, so entity errors remove correct arguments before the relation stage runs. With independent errors the pipeline F1 is about 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.72.

beyond: Not for the exam. Open information extraction drops the fixed relation set and reads a relation phrase straight from the sentence, which scales to the web but needs heavy normalisation later. Neural relation extraction replaces hand features with a CNN or transformer over the sentence or over the dependency path. Joint models predict entities and relations together so that one stage can correct the other. Large language models now extract triples from a prompt with no task-specific training, though scoring them still needs held-out gold triples. Search for open information extraction, joint entity and relation extraction, and knowledge graph construction.
